summary: KS1 (ages 5-7) first encounter with the heart and blood: the heart is a fist-sized muscle, roughly centre-left of the chest, that pumps (squeezes) blood continuously through tubes called blood vessels to every part of the body, and you can feel this pumping as a heartbeat (hand on chest) or pulse (fingers on wrist/neck), which speeds up with activity. Keep depth at 'pump + tubes + you can feel it'; chambers and the double circulation are later content (the circulatory system is introduced from Year 6, and the detailed structure of the heart is often taught later still). This is enrichment, not a graded KS1/early-elementary standard. Activities are embodied and concrete, anchoring every abstract claim in a felt experience, and explicitly correct the valentine-shape, far-left-placement, blue-blood, 'heart only beats with emotions/only beats when you move', 'blood only where you are cut', and heart-is-the-same-as-lungs misconceptions.
misconceptions: Thinking the heart is shaped like the ❤ symbol, rather than a fist-sized muscle.
Believing the heart is on the far left edge of the chest rather than roughly centre-left.
Thinking blood is blue inside the body and turns red only in air — blood is always red.
Believing the heart only 'beats' with emotions (love/fright), not that it pumps blood every second of life.
Thinking blood just sits still in the body or only appears when you are cut, rather than constantly circulating.
Confusing the heartbeat with breathing, or thinking the heart and lungs are the same thing.

activities.title: Be the heart: pump blood around the body
steps: Make a fist and hold it to the centre-left of your chest to show how big your real heart is and where it sits.
Squeeze a soft ball (or tap/press a beating heart on screen) over and over, never stopping, to 'be' the pump.
Watch or imagine each squeeze pushing a pulse of red blood out along the tubes (blood vessels) to the hands, toes, and head, then looping back for the next squeeze.
Place two fingers on your own wrist or neck and find the beat; notice it throbs in time with each pump.
Pretend to go for a run (run on the spot), then feel your pulse again and notice it is faster - the working muscles are asking for more blood, so the heart pumps faster.
activities.insight: The heart is a never-stopping muscle that squeezes blood through tubes to every part of the body right now; the beat you feel at your wrist is that pump working, and it speeds up when you are active.

activities.title: Find it, name it, bust the myths: a body you can explore
steps: On a body outline (or your own body), point to where the real heart is - centre-left of the chest, about the size of your fist.
Compare the real fist-sized heart muscle with the valentine heart symbol and say which one is the real organ and what the real one does.
Find the pulse points at the wrist and neck by pressing gently with two fingers (on one side of the neck only).
Trace the tubes (blood vessels) branching out to the hands, feet and head to show blood reaches everywhere.
Answer 'is blood blue?' and give the correct answer: blood is always red; veins only look blue through the skin.
activities.insight: The heart is a fist-sized muscle (not the valentine shape) sitting centre-left; blood is always red and travels through tubes to every part of the body, and you can find your pulse where those tubes run near the skin.

activities.title: Ask the heart: why do you pound when I run?
steps: Talk with a friendly cartoon heart or school nurse: first find your own pulse, then say what you feel.
Jump or run on the spot, feel your pulse again, and describe out loud what changed.
Explain back, in your own words, why the heart beats faster when you run (the muscles are working harder and need more blood).
activities.insight: Putting the felt experience into your own words - the pump speeds up when your body works harder - can consolidate that the heart responds to what your body is doing.

activities.title: Quick checks: real heart, pulse points, always pumping
steps: Choose the real heart from two pictures (fist-sized muscle vs the valentine symbol).
Tap or point to where you can feel a pulse.
Answer true/false: 'the heart keeps pumping even when you are asleep.'
Answer: if you got a tiny cut on your finger and on your toe, would both bleed? Why?
activities.insight: Checking the basics confirms the child can recognise the real heart, knows where to feel a pulse, and can state that the heart pumps blood everywhere, all the time.

checkQuestion: Right now, sitting still, is your heart beating and is your blood moving — or does that only happen when you run around? And if you got a tiny cut on your finger AND on your toe, why would BOTH bleed? What does that tell you about where your blood is?
checkAnswer: The heart is beating and blood is moving all the time, even sitting still — it beats faster when you run but never stops. Both the finger and the toe bleed because blood travels through tubes (blood vessels) to every part of the body, so blood is everywhere, not only in one spot and not only when you exercise.
